# Pilot — GOV.UK Service Standard assessment reports

**Real data.** Generated by `tools/adapters/projects-govuk-assessments.py` from the GOV.UK
Search API and Content API: all 492 published Service Standard assessment reports, from
2013-12 to 2026-07.

```bash
python3 tools/adapters/projects-govuk-assessments.py --out examples/pilot-govuk-assessments
```

Result: **389 services** (projects), **492 assessments** (each a milestone and an update), 128
organizations, all passing JSON Schema, reference integrity and the SHACL shapes. The adapter
writes three files into this directory and leaves this README alone.

This is the pilot for the `DigitalServicePhase` scheme. The NYC pilot covered capital projects.
This one tests the digital-service lifecycle, milestones and updates against real data.

## What the feed is

A report records one assessment of one digital service at one stage, with a date, a stage and a
result. It is evidence about services, not a project list. Four things the profile expects are
not in it:

- **No service identifier.** A service is recovered by following the "Previous assessment
  reports" links inside each report and grouping the chains. 322 services have one report, 43
  have two, 15 three, 6 four and 3 five. Titles cannot be used: they are inconsistent
  ("HO View or share your DBS result beta assessment report" beside "Register a birth").
- **No usable service name field.** The name is the first paragraph of the report body, or else
  the title with the assessment wording stripped. Both are heuristics. A few names are still
  report titles (for example "Alpha Assessment August 2020").
- **No project status.** None is asserted.
- **No owning department.** The `organisations` metadata is always the Government Digital
  Service, who publish the reports. The owner is the "Service provider" row in each report's
  own table. This is the same trap the services pilot hit.

## The scheme held

`alpha`, `beta` and `live` covered every assessed stage. Nothing needed `discovery` or `retired`,
and nothing needed `private-beta` or `public-beta`: the feed does not distinguish them.
Reassessments and "amber evidence reviews" are assessments of the same stage, so they map to it.

Phases of the 389 services, by latest assessment: alpha 205, beta 149, live 34, none 1.

## Phase is where the service was, not where it is

An assessment is held to decide whether a service may leave a stage. A service assessed at
alpha was in alpha on that date, and what happened next is not in the feed. Of the 205
services last assessed at alpha, 126 passed, so most of them probably moved on to beta without
a later report ever appearing here. So `phase` is the stage of the latest assessment, and each
project carries `dateModified` set to that assessment date. Without the date, `phase: alpha`
would read as a claim about today.

## Results map to milestone status, as a judgement

| Result | Milestone status | Count |
|---|---|---|
| met, green | `met` | 301 |
| amber | `partiallyMet` | 51 |
| not-met, red | `notMet` | 99 |
| blank, `pass`, `criteria` | omitted | 41 |

The mapping is not a GOV.UK rule. OCDS's `partiallyMet` is the nearest of its four values to an
amber result. A milestone with no mappable result is left without a status.

## Two things the milestone model did not fit

- **One date, not two.** An assessment has a single date and a verdict. The profile's `dueDate`
  (scheduled) and `dateMet` (reached) assume a milestone is planned first. The adapter puts the
  assessment date in `dueDate` for every assessment and in `dateMet` as well when the result is
  met or partially met. For `met` milestones the two are always equal, which is accurate but
  odd. A `notMet` milestone has a date and no `dateMet`, correctly.
- **A failed milestone can repeat.** One service has an alpha assessment not met in 2022, partly
  met in 2024, an alpha review met later in 2024, then a beta assessment met in 2026. The
  profile represents all four as separate milestones, which is right, but "alpha assessment" is not
  one milestone with a changing status.

## Updates worked without change

Each report is a schema.org `Article` with `about` pointing at the project, `url`,
`datePublished` and `publisher` (GDS). No `ProjectUpdate` type was needed, and publishing a
report did not require editing the project.

## Source gaps

| Gap | Count |
|---|---|
| no "Service provider" row, so no `parentOrganization` | 37 projects |
| result blank, `pass` or `criteria` | 41 assessments |
| no stage on the latest report, so no phase | 1 project |

## Organizations: resolved against GOV.UK's own register

The service provider is typed by hand: `DWP`, `Department for Work and Pensions`,
`Department for Work and Pensions (DWP)`, `The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP)`,
`Department for Work & Pensions ( DWP )`. Left as written, each becomes its own organization.

GOV.UK publishes a register of its bodies (`/api/organisations`, 1,267 entries with official
title, abbreviation and a stable content id). The adapter resolves each provider against it with
rules that cannot change which body is meant: case, spacing, `&` for `and`, a leading `the`,
and a bracketed abbreviation only when it is the register's own abbreviation for the body named
before it. A match gives the register's record: the official name as `name`, the abbreviation and
every spelling seen as `alternateName`, the register page as `sameAs`, and the same `@id` the
[services pilot](../pilot-govuk-services/) uses for that department, so the two pilots join.

Result: 266 of the 352 projects that name a provider resolve to 55 register bodies. The other
86 stay as written, in 73 organizations, and are counted. They are what a program should not
guess at:

- typos: `Department for Works and Pensions`, `Department for Work and Pension (DWP)`
- old names: `Department for Levelling Up, Housing & Communities`, `DULHC`
- joint or nested owners: `DfT/DVLA`, `Home Office (HMPO)`, `Cabinet Office (Infrastructure Project Authority)`
- not a body: `Department`, `Platforms & Architecture`

A fuzzy match would fix some of these and wrongly merge others. The register approach is only
as good as the publisher's register, and not every publisher has one (see the NYC pilot).

## Selection bias

Only services that were assessed appear. The feed says nothing about services that were never
assessed, were cancelled before assessment, or have since been retired. 34 live services is a
count of assessed live services, not of live services.
